chapter: Postwar: Chicago, Vinson, Hines and Cootie
title: Hearing Chick Webb
summary: He heard Chick Webb in person in Kansas City and again at the Savoy, though they argue about the year Webb died.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: : Oh, you didn't ever -- you didn't ever get to hear Chick, did you?
Chick Webb? Sure.
: Oh, did you?

Sure, the first time I heard Chick in person was in Kansas City. See, he came to Kansas City and we were playing at the College Inn. McShann's band was at the College Inn. They came over to the auditorium. Ella Fitzgerald was with him.
: Oh, yes.
In Kansas City.
: About '42, you mean.
No, '42, we were in New York. This was before.
Yes. Well, you joined the Army in '43.
Yeah. And I got out -- Or '44.
In '45. But so, but, listen, yeah, Chick died in '40 or '41.
No, no.
Yes, he did.
He died in -- (In 1939--ed.)
June, '41.
I thought it was '42.
I don't think so, Gus.
Yeah, see, because Chick was in -- he was also at the Savoy when we were there. When we came to New York, he was still alive. Chick was alive.
And you came to New York with MacShann.
Yeah, we came there in '41.
Well, yeah. Well, I --
And --
Yeah.
So he was alive, because I saw him there at the Savoy.
Well, tell me something. Didn't that give you a kind of a thrill?
Oh, to see him? Sure.
And the sound on his bass drum? He had the foot.
Not only his bass drum, but everything he did.
Well, tell me about it. What kind of way?
Well, the things he played on his drum.
He had very strong wrists, didn't he?
Oh, yeah, he was strong in what he was doing. His accents of beats and all like that.
Because he couldn't read. He couldn't read music at all. He didn't know music at all, but he knew everything he heard. He knew all the arrangements. He knew when anybody was hitting a wrong note.
Well, at the time I didn't know that. I didn't know that.
He was a natural.
Yeah, sure. And --
Do you remember? When he'd open up at the Savoy, he'd go (KNOCKS) -- and the band started. You remember that sound on his drum?
Well, yeah, that's that kickoff, yeah, that's what that was. And everybody knew --
[You'd know] that sound, that sound on the --
And who else --
Did he have those drums tuned? Did he have --
Well, he had them tuned the way he wanted.
Yeah.
Yeah, you tune drums. You can, sure.
That wasn't tympany, was it?
No, just --
No, just the bass drum and you -- the way you tighten it or --
The bass drum, you tighten your tom-toms and all like that. And they tuned those out some. --you can tune
Yeah. But that style that Chick played, that was behind -- the style was behind what you -- because Jo was later, as far as style was concerned, Jo Jones succeeded --
Yeah, Jo came in later.
Yeah, yeah.
Yeah. And --
I just wondered whether it made a real impression on you.
Oh, sure.
Yeah.
It was just happy for me to be in New York and meet all these musicians.
Yeah, yeah, right.
Because I'd never gotten to see every musician that --
No, no.
--I'd hear people talk about them.
